2.text: tion of women’s dress by men. The same purpose is accomplished by a

3.text: change in the cut of the hair; for instance, by arranging a double fringe

4.text: around the crown, closely cropped according to the Chukchee mode, or with

5.text: the addition of an extra tuft on the crown or on the nape of the neck.

6.text: A change of a similar nature is adopted by others also; for instance, by

7.text: a murderer when he wishes to escape the vengeance of his victim, who might

8.text: easily come back in the shape of a keˊlᴇ. If not kept back, this keˊlᴇ will

9.text: possess himself of the murderer and induce him to do further violence in order

10.text: to have him punished by his neighbors for his crimes. The mind of the

11.text: Chukchee can conceive of no other retribution for a crime unavenged by

12.text: the relatives of the victim. The Greek conception of the Furies pursuing the

13.text: unpunished criminal, and driving him to madness and despair, was probably

14.text: also developed from a similar idea of the revengeful “spirit” of the victim

15.text: pursuing its murderer. Besides this, I was told that the murderer must not cut

16.text: his hair at all, but pull it out hair by hair. This process will act as a preven-

17.text: tive against the return of the “desire to kill,” which otherwise is sure to come

18.text: back and incite him to other murders. The “desire to kill,” in this case, is

19.text: probably derived from the same idea of the revengeful “spirit” of the victim

20.text: possessing itself of the mind of the murderer.

21.text: Another measure of like nature is a change of name, which is effected

22.text: by the Chukchee very readily on several occasions of their life. The way

23.text: in which the new-born infant receives its name will be described in a later

24.text: chapter. Then, after a few years, the parents — if they are afraid that the

25.text: name does not suit the little one, making him suffer, “making his bones

26.text: heavy” — proceed to the first change of the name, after which, during later

27.text: life, several other changes may follow. The names thus assumed are of the

28.text: most varied character. Sometimes they are taken from among the usual

29.text: Chukchee names, but more often they are chosen with the view of giving

31.text: Some of these are names of animals, such as Aˊᵋttᴇn (“dog”), Aˊᵋttᴇqäi

32.text: (“small dog”), Keiˊñɪn (“bear”), Êˊᵋhɪlhɪn (“wolf”), etc. Others refer to the

33.text: “alien” tribes, such as Aiˊwan, Eˊtel, Taˊn˙ñɪtan,¹ Roˊčhɪlêᵋn (that on the other

34.text: shore). Proper names taken from the “aliens” are also used for the purpose.

35.text: Some names are even those of spirits, — Keleˊwg̣i (keˊlᴇ-man), Keˊle-ñeˊut

36.text: (“keˊlᴇ-woman”), Kama-taˊhin (“spirit’s limit”); among the Koryak, Kaˊmak

37.text: (“spirit”), etc. Female names are given to men, and vice versâ. Shamans
